experiments.title: The Droop Test: how bendy is it?
experiments.question: Which strips bend the most when they stick out from a table, and which bend the least?
experiments.predict: Line up the strips. Put the one you think is the stiffest first, and the bendiest last.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, cut every strip 2 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres long. Let exactly 10 centimetres stick out over the edge. Tape one coin to the tip of each. Measure each strip 3 times.

materials.item: strips of 2 centimetres by 20 centimetres: an ice cream stick, thin card, thick card, printer paper, kitchen foil folded in three, cotton cloth
one coin, the same one every time
sticky tape
a heavy book to hold the strip down
a 30 centimetre ruler
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Cut the strips with child scissors, or ask a grown-up to cut the card. Do not use anything sharp or splintery.

schedule.what: Guess the order. Measure the drop of each strip 3 times. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart. Draw one bar for each strip. Make each bar as tall as the middle value.
experiments.context: This is the droop test. You push a strip of material out over the edge of a table, and measure how far its tip drops. A big drop means a bendy material. A small drop means a stiff one.

flow.do: 1. Lay the six strips out. 2. Ask your child to put them in a line, stiffest first and bendiest last.
flow.say: Which strip will stay straightest when it sticks out? Which will bend the most? Put them in a line.
flow.kid: Look at the six strips. Put them in a line. Stiffest first, bendiest last. This is your guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the droop test. You find out how bendy each strip is by letting it stick out over a table edge.

flow.do: 1. Lay the first strip on the table. 2. Slide it until exactly 10 centimetres stick out over the edge. 3. Put the heavy book on the other end. 4. Tape the coin to the tip.
flow.say: We let 10 centimetres stick out each time, with the same coin on the tip. Only the strip changes. That makes it a fair test.
flow.kid: Put a strip on the table with 10 centimetres sticking out. Hold the other end under a book. Tape the coin to the tip.
flow.parent: Mark the table edge with a pencil on the book side so that the same length sticks out each time. Use a long ruler held upright against the table edge.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ruler upright against the table edge. 2. Read how far the tip has dropped below the table top. 3. Write it down. 4. Do this 3 times for each strip. If a strip hangs straight down, write 10.
flow.say: The drop is how far the tip goes down from the table top. A small drop means stiff. A big drop means bendy.
flow.kid: Measure how far the tip dropped. Write the number. Do it 3 times for each strip.

chart.title: A ruler, reading the drop of a paper strip in centimetres (cm)
chart.label: Read where the tip of the strip reaches on the ruler.

flow.parent: To find the middle value, put the three numbers in order and take the middle one. If one try is very different, check that the same length stuck out and the coin was taped in the same place.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle values, with one bar for each strip.
flow.say: Each strip gets one bar. The taller the bar, the more the strip bent down.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each strip. A taller bar means a bendier strip.

check.q: In the droop test, a strip with a big drop is…
check.why: A big drop means the strip bent a lot under the coin. That is a flexible strip. A small drop means rigid. Picking 'stronger' mixes up bendy and strong. A very bendy cloth can still be strong.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how far the tip of each strip dropped
chart.note: These numbers are made up. The most a strip can drop here is 10 centimetres, because that is how far it sticks out.

flow.do: Talk about the ice cream stick, thick card and thin paper. They are all made of wood fibres. What changed?
flow.say: Thick card is made of the same stuff as paper. But it bends much less. What changed?
flow.kid: Card and paper are both made of wood fibres. Why does the card bend less?
flow.think: Thickness matters as well as material. How could you test a thick and a thin strip of the same paper?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the ice cream stick is the stiffest and the cloth is the bendiest. What I saw: the stick dropped 1 centimetre and the cloth hung straight down at 10. Why: wood fibres packed together resist bending, and cloth threads slide and fold.

experiments.title: How Much Can It Hold? The strength test
experiments.question: Which strip holds the most weight before it tears?
experiments.predict: Line up the strips. Put the one you think is weakest first, and the strongest last.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, cut every strip 2 centimetres wide and 25 centimetres long. Use the same marbles, added one at a time, the same gentle way. Test each strip 3 times with a new strip each time, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: strips 2 centimetres wide and 25 centimetres long, three of each: newspaper, printer paper, chart paper, cotton cloth, plastic carry bag
a small paper cup and a paper clip
sticky tape
30 or more marbles, or identical small stones
a cushion or folded towel
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Put a cushion under the cup so nothing hits the floor or your feet. Pick up every marble you drop, because they roll. Marbles are not for children under 3.

schedule.what: Guess the order. Hang a cup from each strip and add marbles until it tears. Do it 3 times. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart. Draw one bar for each strip. Make each bar as tall as the middle value.
experiments.context: This is the strength test. You tape a strip of material under a table edge, hang a cup from it, and add marbles one at a time until the strip tears. The more marbles it holds, the stronger it is.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the five kinds of strip. 2. Ask your child to put them in a line, weakest first and strongest last.
flow.say: Which strip do you think is the weakest? Which is the strongest? Put them in a line, weakest first.
flow.kid: Look at the five kinds of strip. Put them in a line. Weakest first, strongest last. This is your guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the strength test. You find out how strong each material is by hanging weights from a strip of it.

flow.do: 1. Tape 3 centimetres of one strip to the underside of a table edge. 2. Tape 3 centimetres at the bottom to the paper cup's rim, through a paper clip hook, so the cup hangs free. 3. Put the cushion under the cup.
flow.say: The cup hangs from the strip. We will add marbles one at a time. The strip that holds the most is the strongest.
flow.kid: Tape a strip under the table edge. Hang the paper cup from the bottom. Put the cushion under the cup.
flow.parent: If the tape peels off instead of the strip tearing, do not count that try. Press the tape down firmly and use the same length of tape each time.

flow.do: 1. Add one marble at a time, gently. 2. Count out loud. 3. When the strip tears, write down how many marbles were in the cup. 4. Do it 3 times for each kind of strip, with a new strip each time.
flow.say: Drop each marble in gently, the same way every time. Count out loud. Write down the number when the strip tears.
flow.kid: Drop in one marble at a time. Count out loud. Write the number when the strip tears.
flow.parent: Let a young child count while you drop the marbles in. The plastic bag will stretch a lot before it tears. That is worth noticing.

flow.do: Help your child find the middle value of the 3 tries for each strip. Then draw a bar chart.
flow.say: Put the three numbers in order. The middle one is the middle value. Then draw a bar for each strip.
flow.kid: Find the middle number of your three tries. Draw one bar for each strip.

check.q: A strip held 11, 10 and 11 marbles in three tries. What does that tell you?
options: The result is reliable, because the numbers are close
check.why: When repeated tries give nearly the same number, the result is reliable. That means we can trust it. Picking 'useless' is the opposite. It is when the three numbers are far apart that we should worry.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how many marbles each strip held before it tore
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Talk about the plastic bag. It held the most, but it also stretched a lot. Is stretchy the same as strong?
flow.say: The plastic bag stretched and stretched before it tore. Does that mean it is strong, or only stretchy?
flow.kid: The plastic bag stretched a lot. Is stretchy the same as strong?

ask.q: What would happen if you tested thick paper in the same way?
good: It would hold more, because there is more paper.
Thickness matters too, so we cut all the strips to the same width.

flow.think: If a thick strip holds more than a thin one of the same paper, how can we compare two different materials fairly?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the plastic bag is the strongest and newspaper the weakest. What I saw: the bag held 22 marbles and the newspaper held only 5. Why: plastic is made of long, strong chains that are hard to pull apart, and paper is made of short fibres that slip.

experiments.title: Thirsty Squares: which soaks up the most?
experiments.question: Which material soaks up the most water?
experiments.predict: Line up the five squares. Put the one you think is least thirsty first, and the thirstiest last.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, cut every square 10 centimetres by 10 centimetres. Use the same teaspoon, filled level, and wait the same 10 seconds each time. Test each square 3 times, drying the plate in between.

materials.item: squares 10 centimetres by 10 centimetres: paper towel, newspaper, cotton cloth, kitchen sponge, plastic carry bag
a teaspoon
a cup of water
a flat plate, and a cloth to dry it
a watch or phone with seconds
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Wipe up spilt water so no one slips.

schedule.what: Guess the order. Add water one teaspoon at a time to each square. Do it 3 times. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart. Draw one bar for each square. Make each bar as tall as the middle value.
experiments.context: This is the thirsty squares test. You add water to a small square of material one teaspoon at a time. The number of teaspoons it soaks up before water sits on top shows how absorbent it is.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the five squares. 2. Ask your child to put them in a line, least thirsty first.
flow.say: Which square will soak up the most water? Which will soak up the least? Put them in a line.
flow.kid: Look at the five squares. Put them in a line. Least thirsty first. This is your guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the thirsty squares test. You find out which material is most absorbent. Absorbent means it soaks up liquid.

flow.do: 1. Put a square flat on the plate. 2. Fill a teaspoon level with water. 3. Pour it onto the middle of the square.
flow.say: We pour one level teaspoon in the middle of the square. Then we count slowly to ten, and watch.
flow.kid: Put a square on the plate. Pour one level teaspoon of water in the middle. Count to ten.
flow.parent: Fill the spoon to the same level each time. Pour in the middle, not near an edge.

flow.do: 1. After 10 seconds, look at the square. 2. If no water is sitting on top, add another teaspoon. 3. Stop when water first stays on top for 10 seconds. 4. Write down how many teaspoons it soaked up, not counting the last one. 5. Do each square 3 times, drying the plate each time.
flow.say: If the water disappears into the square, add another teaspoon. Stop when some water stays sitting on top. Count the teaspoons that disappeared.
flow.kid: Add one teaspoon at a time. Stop when water stays on top. Write how many disappeared.
flow.parent: The plastic bag will soak up none. Write 0. That is a result too. A zero tells us the bag is waterproof.

flow.do: Help your child find the middle value for each square and draw a bar chart.
flow.say: Each square gets one bar. The taller the bar, the thirstier the square.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each square. A taller bar means it soaks up more water.

check.q: The plastic bag square soaked up 0 teaspoons. What does that tell you about plastic?
check.why: A result of 0 is a proper result. Water sat on top at once, so the plastic did not let water in. That is waterproof. Picking 'the test did not work' is a common reaction to a zero. Zero is an answer.

flow.do: Look closely at the sponge and the plastic through a magnifying glass. Then dip the edge of a strip of paper towel in a cup of water and watch the water climb.
flow.say: Look at the sponge. It is full of tiny holes. Now dip a strip of paper towel in water. Watch the water climb up. That is called wicking.
flow.kid: Look at the sponge closely. It has tiny holes. Dip a paper towel edge in water. Watch the water climb.
flow.think: Why does water climb up through the paper towel, even though gravity pulls it down?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the sponge is the thirstiest and the plastic bag is not absorbent at all. What I saw: the sponge soaked up 8 teaspoons and the bag soaked up none. Why: the sponge is full of tiny gaps that pull water in, and plastic has no gaps.

experiments.title: The Ice Race: heat carriers and heat blockers
experiments.question: Which material carries heat into ice the fastest, and which carries it the slowest?
experiments.predict: Put your hand on each material and decide which feels coldest. Then guess which one will melt an ice cube the fastest.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use ice cubes of the same size from the same tray. Put them down at the same moment, in the same room, away from sun and fans. Put the ice in the middle of each material.
results_table: Time when the cube was gone (minutes)

materials.item: a steel plate or thali
a plastic lid or plastic plate
a wooden chopping board
a thickly folded woollen scarf or blanket
four ice cubes of the same size
a clock with minutes, or a phone timer
a thermometer, if you have one
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Wipe up any melted water at once so no one slips.

schedule.what: Feel the plates and guess. Put the ice down. Check every five minutes. Write down the times. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each material. Make each bar as tall as its melting time.
experiments.context: This is the ice race. You put identical ice cubes on different materials, and time how long each cube takes to melt. Heat from the room flows into the ice. A material that carries heat quickly melts the ice faster.

flow.do: 1. Lay the four materials on a table where they have sat for an hour. 2. Ask your child to put a palm on each for 10 seconds. 3. Ask which feels coldest.
flow.say: Put your hand flat on each one. Count to ten. Which feels the coldest? Which feels the warmest?
flow.kid: Put your palm on each one for ten seconds. Which feels coldest? Which feels warmest?
flow.context: This is the first step of the ice race. First you feel the materials with your hand, then you time ice melting on them to see what is really going on.

ask.q: Do you think the coldest one is really colder than the others?
good: Maybe it is just the same temperature.
I do not know yet. Let us find out.

flow.parent: If you have a thermometer, check each material now. They will all show nearly the same number. Keep that result to look at later.

flow.do: 1. Take four ice cubes from the same tray at the same time. 2. Put one in the middle of each material. 3. Start the timer.
flow.say: We will put an ice cube on each one at the same moment. Heat from the room flows into the ice and melts it. We will see which one lets the heat flow fastest.
flow.kid: Put one ice cube in the middle of each material. Start the timer.
flow.parent: Place the folded wool so the cube sits on top of it. A thick fold is the best insulator. Keep all four in the same part of the room.

flow.do: 1. Every 5 minutes, look at each cube. 2. When a cube is gone, write down the time. 3. Do something else while you wait. 4. Write the time for all four.
flow.say: Check each cube every five minutes. Write down when it is all gone. While you wait, do something else.
flow.kid: Check the ice every five minutes. Write down when each cube is gone.
flow.parent: If the room is cold, the race will be slow. You can stop after 40 minutes and note how much ice is left on each. A bigger piece left means a slower melter.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the melting times.
flow.say: Each material gets a bar. The taller the bar, the longer the ice lasted.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each material. A taller bar means the ice lasted longer.

check.q: The ice melted fastest on the steel plate. Why?
options: Steel carried the room's heat into the ice fastest
check.why: Steel is a good conductor of heat, so it let heat flow from the room into the ice quickly. Picking 'the steel plate was colder' is the common idea. If the steel was colder, the ice would have lasted longer. Steel makes no heat by itself either.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how many minutes each ice cube took to melt
chart.x: What the ice cube sat on
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your times will depend on how warm the room is. The order matters more than the numbers.

flow.do: Compare the melting times with the hand test. The steel felt coldest. Was it really colder than the wooden board?
flow.say: Your hand said the steel was coldest. But the steel melted the ice fastest. So it was not colder. It moved heat faster.
flow.kid: The steel felt cold, but it melted ice the fastest. So the steel was not colder. It moves heat faster.
flow.think: So when your hand says 'cold', what is it really telling you?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: steel carries heat fastest and wool carries it slowest. What I saw: ice on steel was gone in 14 minutes and on wool it took 38. Why: steel is a conductor, and wool traps air, and air is a poor conductor.

experiments.title: Layers to Darkness: transparent, translucent or opaque?
experiments.question: How many layers of each material does it take to stop a torch's light?
experiments.predict: Guess how many layers of butter paper it will take before the light disappears from the wall.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same torch, the same distance from the wall and the same dim room each time. Add one layer at a time. Count the layers when the light spot on the wall just disappears.

materials.item: a torch
a plain wall in a dim room, or in the evening
15 sheets of butter paper or tracing paper
10 sheets of tissue paper
a thin cotton cloth, and some sheets of newspaper
a clear glass or plastic cup, a steel plate and a piece of cardboard
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Do not shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Sort the materials with a torch. Then add layers until the light disappears. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart. Draw one bar for each material. Make each bar as tall as the number of layers.
experiments.context: In this experiment you shine a torch through different materials onto a wall. First you sort them as transparent, translucent or opaque. Then you add layers one at a time to see how many it takes to block the light.

flow.do: 1. Dim the room. 2. Shine the torch on the wall. 3. Hold each of the cup, the butter paper, the cloth, the steel plate and the cardboard in front of the torch. 4. Sort each one: transparent, translucent or opaque.
flow.say: Hold each thing in front of the torch. Transparent means a clear bright spot. Translucent means a blurry glow. Opaque means just a shadow.
flow.kid: Hold each thing in front of the torch. Is the spot on the wall clear, blurry or gone? Sort them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the layers experiment. You use a torch to sort materials into transparent, translucent and opaque.
flow.parent: Good answers: the cup is transparent, the butter paper and thin cloth are translucent, the steel plate and cardboard are opaque.

flow.do: 1. Hold one sheet of butter paper in front of the torch. 2. Note the glow on the wall. 3. Add a second sheet. 4. Keep adding, one at a time, counting.
flow.say: Add one sheet at a time and watch the glow. Count the sheets. Stop when the light spot is just gone.
flow.kid: Add one sheet at a time. Count them. Stop when the light is gone.

ask.q: What do you notice as you add more layers?
good: The light gets dimmer.
The glow gets smaller.
It goes from translucent to opaque.

flow.do: Repeat with tissue paper, thin cloth and newspaper. Write down the number of layers for each.
flow.say: Now do the same with tissue paper, cloth and newspaper. Which one blocks the light with the fewest layers?
flow.kid: Do the same with tissue paper, cloth and newspaper. Count the layers each time.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the layers for each material.
flow.say: Each material gets a bar. A taller bar means it took more layers to block the light.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each material. A taller bar means more layers.

check.q: One sheet of butter paper is translucent. A tall stack is opaque. What does this show?
options: Translucent or opaque can depend on thickness
check.why: Each layer scatters and soaks up some light. One layer leaves lots, so it is translucent. A tall stack leaves none, so it is opaque. Picking 'the atoms change' is a nice thought, but the atoms are the same. We simply added more of them in the way of the light.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how many layers it took to block the torch light
chart.y: Layers until no light came through
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different, and depend on your torch and your paper.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: more layers make a material more opaque. What I saw: one butter paper let a glow through, but 5 layers stopped it. Why: each layer scatters and soaks up some light, so the more layers there are, the less gets through.

activities.title: Feely Bag Detective

materials.item: a cloth bag or pillowcase
8 small things: a steel spoon, a wooden spoon, a rubber band, a cotton ball, a smooth stone, a glass marble, a sponge, a key

activities.safety: Use nothing sharp, nothing breakable and nothing small enough for a young child to swallow.

schedule.what: Describe things by touch, using only property words. Then guess.

activities.record: Write down the three property words that gave the best clue for each thing.
activities.context: In this game you feel things you cannot see, inside a bag, and describe them with property words only. A friend then guesses what they are.

flow.do: 1. Put the eight things in the bag without your child looking. 2. Explain: they will feel one thing at a time and describe it only with property words. They may not say what it is.
flow.say: Put a hand in the bag and feel one thing. Tell me what it is like. You may say hard, soft, cold, smooth, rough, bendy. You may not say its name.
flow.kid: Feel one thing in the bag. Tell what it is like. Do not say its name.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Feely Bag Detective game. You use only touch, and property words, to describe hidden things.

flow.do: 1. Your child describes a thing in the bag using only property words. 2. You guess what it is. 3. Swap roles. 4. Play until all 8 things are out.
flow.say: Tell me three things about it. Hard or soft? Smooth or rough? Cold or warm? Then I will guess.
flow.kid: Describe the thing with three property words. Your partner guesses. Then swap.

good: Cold and hard together tell it is metal.
Bendy and springy tell it is rubber.
Soft and fluffy tell it is cotton.

flow.parent: Praise exact words. 'Smooth, cold, hard' is better than 'nice'. If your child stops at one word, ask for two more.

flow.do: Take out the steel spoon and the wooden spoon. Ask your child to hold one in each hand, eyes closed. Ask which feels colder.
flow.say: Hold one in each hand. Which feels colder? Now open your eyes. Have they been in the same room all day?
flow.kid: Hold a steel spoon in one hand and a wooden spoon in the other. Which feels colder?

check.q: A steel spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon, in the same room. What does that tell you?
options: Steel carries heat away from your hand faster
check.why: Both are at room temperature. Steel takes heat from your hand faster than wood does, so your skin says 'cold'. Picking 'steel is a lower temperature' is the common idea. A thermometer would show the same number for both. Wood makes no heat of its own.

flow.do: Talk about which senses helped. Touch was used here, but ask what other senses could tell us about a material.
flow.say: We used touch. What other senses help us find out about a material? What can looking tell us? Listening?
flow.kid: Touch told us a lot. What could your eyes and ears tell you about a material?
flow.think: Your skin said the steel was cold. Was your skin right or wrong?

setup.caption: 2. Tell what it is like. Do not say its name.

activities.title: The Property Passport

materials.item: a steel tumbler or tiffin box
a kadhai or pan with a wooden or plastic handle, or a photo of one
a sheet of paper folded into a small booklet
a pencil

schedule.what: Fill in a property passport for one object. Then find the two materials in a pan.

activities.record: A passport page for one object, with the answer to each question.
activities.context: In this activity you make a passport for one everyday object. You find out its properties, one by one, and learn the difference between an object and its material.

flow.do: 1. Fold the paper into a booklet. 2. Choose the steel tumbler. 3. On the first page write: Object: steel tumbler. Material: steel.
flow.say: An object is a single thing with a shape and a use. A material is what it is made of. Let's write both on the first page.
flow.kid: Choose the steel tumbler. Write: Object, steel tumbler. Material, steel.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Property Passport. A passport tells you about a traveller. This one tells you about a material.
flow.parent: Say again, in plain words: the tumbler is the object. Steel is the material. The tumbler's shape is a property of the object. The steel's properties would be the same in a spoon or a sheet.

flow.do: Fill in the passport with these questions. Hard or soft? Rigid or flexible? Shiny or dull? Rough or smooth? See-through or not? Waterproof or absorbent? Cold to touch or not? Does it ring when tapped? Does it float? Write one answer for each.
flow.say: Let's ask the tumbler these questions one by one. For each, look, touch or try it. Then write the answer.
flow.kid: Ask the tumbler each question. Look, touch or try it. Write the answers in the passport.
flow.parent: Expected answers for steel: hard, rigid, shiny, smooth, opaque, waterproof, cold to touch, rings when tapped, sinks (but a hollow tumbler will float for a moment if set down gently on water).

flow.do: Now look at the kadhai. Ask: how many materials is it made of? Make a passport entry for each one.
flow.say: A kadhai has a steel bowl and a wooden handle. Two materials in one object. Do they have the same properties?
flow.kid: Look at the kadhai. It has two materials. Write a passport entry for each.

ask.q: Why are the two materials different?
good: The bowl must carry heat, so it is steel.
The handle must not carry heat, so it is wood or plastic.

check.q: A kadhai has a steel bowl and a wooden handle. Which is true?
options: One object, two materials, with different properties
check.why: The kadhai is one object. It is made of two materials, steel and wood. They have different properties, and that is why each is used where it is. Picking 'one material' misses the wood. The object and its materials are different ideas.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose another object at home and make a passport at another time.
flow.say: Which object would you like to make a passport for next? Look for one with more than one material.
flow.kid: Pick another object at home. Make a passport for it later.
flow.think: Which property did you find hardest to decide? Why was it hard?

activities.title: The Property Ladder and the Two-Ring Sort

materials.item: a piece of string and some clothes pegs
8 to 12 small things from home, such as a spoon, a pencil, a leaf, a rubber, a coin, a tumbler, a cloth
two skipping ropes or two loops of string
paper labels and a pencil

schedule.what: Put things in order on a washing-line ladder. Then sort them into two overlapping rings.

activities.record: Draw your ladder and your two rings, and write the numbers in each part.
activities.context: In this activity you sort things by their properties in two ways. First you put six things in order on a line. Then you sort them into two overlapping rings. Both are ways of comparing materials.

flow.do: 1. Choose six things. 2. Stretch a string across a doorway like a washing line. 3. Label one end 'hardest' and the other end 'softest'.
flow.say: We will put these six things in order from hardest to softest. Use what you know about scratching and pressing.
flow.kid: Choose six things. Stretch the string. One end is hardest. The other end is softest.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Property Ladder. You put things in order on a line, from the most to the least of one property, like hardness.

flow.do: 1. Your child pegs the six things on the line in order of hardness. 2. Test any pair that is hard to decide. 3. Now take them down and do it again for bendiness.
flow.say: Is the spoon harder than the leaf? How can you check? Test each pair that you are not sure of.
flow.kid: Peg the things in order, hardest to softest. Test any pair you are unsure about. Then try bendiness.

ask.q: Did the order stay the same for hard and bendy?
good: No. A steel spoon is hard but a spoon is not bendy.
A rubber is soft and bendy, but a coin is hard and not bendy.

flow.parent: The point is that the order changes with the property. A thing can be near the top for one property and near the bottom for another.

flow.do: 1. Lay two ropes on the floor as two rings that overlap in the middle. 2. Label one ring HARD and the other SHINY. 3. Your child puts each thing in the right place: in HARD only, in SHINY only, in both, or outside both.
flow.say: Where does a steel spoon go? It is hard and shiny, so it goes where the rings overlap. Where does a wooden spoon go?
flow.kid: Make two rings that overlap. One is HARD. One is SHINY. Put each thing in the right place.
flow.parent: Things that are neither go outside both rings. Some things are hard to decide. Ask your child to say why.

flow.do: Count the things in each part. Write the numbers. Ask: how many are hard? How many are shiny? How many are hard and shiny? How many are neither?
flow.say: Count the things in each part of the rings. How many are hard? How many are both? How many are neither?
flow.kid: Count the things in each part. Write the numbers down.

check.q: A steel spoon is hard and shiny. In the two rings, where does it go?
options: In the part where the rings overlap
check.why: The overlap holds things that have both properties. A steel spoon is hard and shiny, so it goes in the middle. Picking 'HARD only' leaves out the shine. Picking 'outside' means thinking it has neither property.

flow.do: Look at the rings. Ask: could you sort the same things with a different pair of properties? Say which pair.
flow.say: Choose a different pair of properties, like bendy and see-through. How would the things move?
flow.kid: Pick two new properties. How would the things move around the rings?
flow.think: The same things can be sorted in many ways. How do we decide which way is the best?

activities.title: The Gong in Your Ears

materials.item: a piece of string about 1 metre long
a steel spoon, a steel ladle or fork, a wooden spoon and a plastic spoon
a timer

activities.safety: Tap gently. Do not put anything hard in your ears. The string only touches the outside of the ear.

schedule.what: Hang spoons from string and listen. Time how long each rings.

activities.record: Write how many seconds each spoon rang for.
activities.context: In this activity you tie a spoon to a string and listen to it ring against your ears. You find out which materials ring and which only thud. This is another property of materials.

flow.do: 1. Tie the steel spoon in the middle of the string. 2. Hold the two ends of the string, one in each hand. 3. Press the ends against the outside of your ears. 4. Lean forward and let the spoon swing and tap a table edge.
flow.say: Press the string ends gently against your ears. Lean forward until the spoon taps the table. Listen. What do you hear?
flow.kid: Hold the string ends to your ears. Lean over. Let the spoon tap the table. Listen!
flow.context: This is the first step of The Gong in Your Ears. A spoon hung from string makes a surprising sound when you listen through the string.
flow.parent: Most people hear a deep sound like a temple gong or a bell. It is far louder and longer than the plain tap you hear through the air.

flow.do: 1. Swap the steel spoon for the wooden spoon, then the plastic spoon. 2. Tap each against the table the same way. 3. Time how long each one keeps ringing, in seconds. 4. Write the numbers down.
flow.say: Try the wooden spoon. Then the plastic one. Which ring the longest? Which stop at once? Let's time them.
flow.kid: Try each spoon. Which rings the longest? Time each one.

chart.title: Made-up example: how long each spoon rang

flow.do: Talk about why the steel spoon rings and the wooden one does not.
flow.say: When you tap the steel spoon, it shakes back and forth very fast. That shaking is a vibration. Steel keeps shaking for a long time, because it is stiff and springy. Wood soaks up the shaking quickly.
flow.kid: Steel shakes for a long time when you tap it. That makes the ring. Wood stops shaking quickly.

check.q: Why does a brass bell ring for a long time?
options: It is stiff and springy, so it keeps shaking
It is heavy, so it falls slowly
It is hollow, so it is full of echoes
check.why: A bell rings because it keeps vibrating after being hit. Stiff, springy metals like brass keep vibrating for a long time. Soft or squashy materials soak up the shaking and stop. Picking 'hollow echoes' is a common idea. A solid metal spoon rings too, so hollowness is not needed.

flow.do: Ask: which materials in your kitchen would make the best bell? Try tapping a steel plate, a glass tumbler and a cup.
flow.say: If you were making a bell, which material would you choose? Try tapping a steel plate and a glass tumbler. Which sounds best?
flow.kid: Which would make the best bell? Try tapping a steel plate and a glass tumbler.
flow.think: Why do you think temple bells in India are made of bronze or brass, and not of wood?

activities.title: Dance of the Three Veils

materials.item: a clear plastic sheet or a very thin chiffon dupatta
a cotton dupatta or a sheet of butter paper
a tray or a sheet of cardboard
music

activities.safety: Clear a space so no one trips. Do not wrap a veil around anyone's head.

schedule.what: Dance behind three different veils and call the words.

activities.record: Draw the three veils and write transparent, translucent or opaque under each.
activities.context: In this movement game you dance behind three different veils. You feel what transparent, translucent and opaque mean with your whole body.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the three props. 2. Explain the three calls. CLEAR means dance behind the clear sheet. MIST means dance behind the cotton. HIDE means dance behind the tray.
flow.say: When I call 'clear', dance behind the clear sheet. When I call 'mist', dance behind the cotton. When I call 'hide', dance behind the tray.
flow.kid: Three calls. CLEAR, MIST, HIDE. Each one means a different veil.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dance of the Three Veils. A veil is a thin cloth held in front of you. Each veil shows light in a different way.

flow.do: 1. Play music. 2. Call the words in any order. 3. Your child dances behind the right veil. 4. You watch and say what you can see of them.
flow.say: Behind the clear sheet, I can see everything. Behind the cotton, I see a shape. Behind the tray, I see nothing. Let us dance!
flow.kid: Dance behind the veil you are called to. Your partner tells what they can see.

ask.q: What could I see through each veil?
good: Clear: everything.
Mist: only a blurry shape.
Hide: nothing at all.

flow.do: Swap. Your child calls the words and you dance. Talk about what changed.
flow.say: Now you call, and I will dance. Which veil is best for hiding? Which is best for watching?
flow.kid: Swap places. You call the words now.

check.q: Early morning fog is thin. You can see a tree through it, but it looks blurry. Fog is…
check.why: Light gets through the fog but is scattered, so the tree looks blurry. That is translucent. Thin air would be transparent. Very thick fog can become almost opaque. Picking 'transparent' means thinking blurry is the same as clear.

flow.do: Draw the three veils and write transparent, translucent or opaque under each.
flow.say: Draw the three veils. Write a word under each one.
flow.kid: Draw the three veils. Write a word under each.
flow.think: Which of the three would you choose for a window? Which for a curtain? Which for a door?

activities.title: The Kitchen Float Lab

materials.item: a big bowl or bucket of water
a cork, a steel nail, a plastic lid, a stone, a grape, a wooden spoon, an orange with its peel on
two same-sized pieces of kitchen foil, and a lump of plasticine or dough
a towel

activities.safety: Wipe up spilt water. A child should never be left alone near a bucket of water.

schedule.what: Guess float or sink. Test each thing. Then change a material's shape and test again.

activities.record: Make a table: thing, my guess, what happened.
activities.context: In this activity you guess whether things will float or sink in water, and then test them. You also find out that the same material can float in one shape and sink in another.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bowl with water. 2. Lay the things out. 3. For each thing, your child guesses: float or sink. 4. Write the guesses in a table.
flow.say: Here are some things. For each one, guess: will it float or will it sink? Write your guess down.
flow.kid: Look at each thing. Guess: float or sink? Write your guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Float Lab. Float means stays on top of water. Sink means goes to the bottom.

flow.do: 1. Place each thing gently in the water, one at a time. 2. Watch and note what happens. 3. Write it in the table. 4. Peel the orange and test it again.
flow.say: Place each thing gently in the water. Does it float or sink? Peel the orange and try again. Surprised?
flow.kid: Test each thing. Write what happens. Then peel the orange and test it again.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.parent: An orange with its peel floats because the peel holds tiny pockets of air. Without the peel, it is more packed than water and sinks. Many children are surprised.

flow.do: 1. Roll one piece of foil into a tight ball. 2. Shape the other piece into a little boat with high sides. 3. Test both. 4. Do the same with the plasticine.
flow.say: Same foil, same weight. One ball, one boat. Which one will float? Try it.
flow.kid: Roll one piece of foil into a ball. Shape the other into a boat. Test both. What happens?

check.q: A foil ball sinks and a foil boat floats. Both are the same foil. Why?
options: The boat holds air, so it is less packed than water
The ball is a different material
check.why: The boat has a hollow space full of air, so the boat and its air together are less packed than water. The ball is solid foil, more packed than water, so it sinks. They weigh the same, so 'lighter' is wrong. The material is the same, so 'different material' is wrong. The shape of the object is what changed.

flow.do: Talk about how a heavy steel ship floats. Ask your child to work out how it is like the foil boat.
flow.say: A ship weighs thousands of tonnes. But it floats. How is it like the foil boat?
flow.kid: A heavy steel ship floats. How is it like your foil boat?
flow.think: Ice floats on water. What does that tell you about how its pieces are packed?

setup.caption: 1. Guess for each thing: float or sink?

setup.caption: 2. Test each thing. Peel the orange and test it again.

activities.title: Drops on Everything

materials.item: a teaspoon or a dropper
a cup of water
things to test: a colocasia (arbi) leaf, a piece of waxed paper or butter paper, a steel plate, a plastic bag, a cotton cloth, a paper towel, a wooden board
black pepper and a drop of dish soap
a plate

schedule.what: Put one drop on each surface and watch. Then try the pepper and soap trick.

activities.record: Draw each surface and what the drop did: beaded up, spread out, or soaked in.
activities.context: In this activity you put one drop of water on lots of different surfaces. You watch whether it beads up, spreads or soaks in. Then you try a trick that shows the skin on water.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the seven surfaces. 2. Ask your child to guess for each: will the drop bead up, spread out or soak in?
flow.say: A drop of water can do three things. It can stay in a round bead. It can spread out flat. Or it can soak in. Guess what it does on each one.
flow.kid: Guess for each one. Will the drop bead up, spread out or soak in?
flow.context: This is the first step of Drops on Everything. You put a drop of water on different surfaces to learn about waterproof and absorbent materials.

flow.do: 1. Put one drop on each surface. 2. Look from the side. 3. Write: bead, spread or soak. 4. Look at the colocasia leaf with a magnifying glass.
flow.say: Put one drop on each. Look from the side. On the arbi leaf, the drop looks like a tiny silver ball. Why do you think it does that?
flow.kid: Put one drop on each surface. Look from the side. Is it a bead, a spread or a soak?

chart.title: Made-up example: what the drop did

flow.parent: Colocasia leaves are covered in tiny wax bumps. Water cannot spread on them, so it rolls into balls and carries dust away. Lotus leaves do the same.

flow.do: 1. Fill a plate with water. 2. Shake a pinch of pepper on top so it floats. 3. Dip a finger in dish soap. 4. Touch the water in the middle of the plate.
flow.say: Pepper floats on the water. Now touch the middle with a soapy finger. What happens?
flow.kid: Sprinkle pepper on water. Touch the middle with a soapy finger. Watch!
flow.parent: The pepper rushes to the edge. Water's surface acts like a stretchy skin. Soap weakens the skin where it touches, and the strong skin around pulls the pepper away. Agnes Pockels studied this kind of thing in her kitchen in the 1880s.

check.q: A drop of water beads up on a plastic bag. What does that show?
check.why: A bead means the water cannot get in or spread out. That is waterproof. Picking 'absorbent' is the opposite, because an absorbent material would soak the drop up. Heavy has nothing to do with water.

flow.do: Sort the surfaces into three groups: bead, spread, soak. Ask which is useful for a raincoat, which for a towel, which for a plate.
flow.say: Sort the surfaces into bead, spread and soak. Which would you choose for a raincoat? A towel?
flow.kid: Sort the surfaces into three groups. Which is best for a raincoat? Which for a towel?
flow.think: Why do you think plants have waxy leaves? What would happen if a leaf soaked up all the rain?

activities.title: Stretch and Snap

materials.item: a thick rubber band, a hair tie, a strip of plastic bag and a piece of cotton thread, all the same starting length
a paper cup, a paper clip and sticky tape
10 marbles
a 30 centimetre ruler

activities.safety: Do not stretch a rubber band near anyone's face or eyes. Keep the stretch small so it cannot snap back at you.

schedule.what: Hang weights from four things and measure how much each stretches. Then try the warm rubber band trick.

activities.record: Write the starting length and the stretched length for each thing, and subtract.
activities.context: In this activity you hang the same weight from a rubber band, a hair tie, a plastic strip and a thread, and measure how much each stretches. You find out that stretchy and strong are different.

flow.do: 1. Tape the top of the first thing to the underside of a table edge. 2. Measure its length with a ruler. 3. Write it down.
flow.say: Hang the rubber band from the table edge. Measure how long it is now, with nothing on it. Write the number.
flow.kid: Tape the rubber band to the table edge. Measure its length. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stretch and Snap. You measure how much different materials stretch under the same weight. Stretchy means it gets longer when pulled and springs back.

flow.do: 1. Hang the paper cup from the bottom. 2. Add 10 marbles gently. 3. Measure the new length. 4. Subtract the starting length. That is the stretch. 5. Repeat with each other thing.
flow.say: Add ten marbles. Measure again. The stretch is the new length minus the old length. Do the same for each thing.
flow.kid: Hang the cup. Add ten marbles. Measure again. The stretch is the new length minus the old.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how much longer each one got with 10 marbles
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Look at the results. Ask: which stretched the most? Which would you trust to hold a heavy bag?
flow.say: The thread hardly stretched. Does that mean it is weak? Look at the numbers.
flow.kid: Which stretched the most? Which would hold a heavy bag?

check.q: A rubber band stretched a lot. A cotton thread stretched very little. What can you say?
options: The rubber band is stretchier. That does not tell us which is stronger
check.why: Stretchy means gets longer when pulled. Strong means holds a big pull without breaking. They are different. A thin thread can hold a lot of weight and hardly stretch. Picking 'rubber band is stronger' mixes up the two properties.

flow.do: Hold a thick rubber band in both hands and stretch it quickly. Touch it to your lip. Then let it go quickly and touch it to your lip again.
flow.say: Stretch the band fast and touch it to your lip. Now let it relax and touch it to your lip again. What do you feel?
flow.kid: Stretch the band fast. Touch it to your lip. Let it go. Touch again. What do you feel?
flow.parent: The band feels slightly warm when stretched and slightly cool after it relaxes. The long chains of atoms in the rubber uncoil when pulled, and this changes how much the atoms jiggle, which changes the heat. This was noticed by the English scientist John Gough in 1805. Keep the stretch small and your face away from the line of the band.

setup.caption: 1. Hang the band from a table. Measure its length.

setup.caption: 2. Add ten marbles. Measure again. The stretch is the difference.

projects.title: Make Your Own Property Trumps

materials.item: your results tables and bar charts from the experiments
8 stiff paper cards, the size of playing cards
pencils, a ruler and coloured pens
the materials from the experiments, for any new tests

projects.safety: Follow the safety notes of each test you repeat.

schedule.what: Choose 8 materials. Gather your results. Test any that are missing.
Turn your results into scores from 0 to 5. Make the cards.
Play your deck. Compare it with the rough deck and find where they differ.

projects.record: Eight cards, each with a material, a picture and five scores from 0 to 5. Plus a note on what surprised you.
projects.context: In this 3-day project you turn your own measurements into a card game. Each card has real scores for a material, from the tests you did. It is your own set of Property Trumps.

flow.do: 1. Look at your tables from the scratch, droop, strength, thirsty squares, ice race and layers tests. 2. Choose 8 materials that appear in several tests. 3. Write them in a big table.
flow.say: You have done many tests. Let's collect the numbers in one big table. One row for each material, one column for each test.
flow.kid: Look at your results. Choose 8 materials. Put their numbers in one big table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Property Trumps project. You gather all your measurements into one table, one row for each material.
flow.parent: Not every material appears in every test. That is fine. This is the moment to fill the gaps by testing the missing ones, using the same method as before.

flow.do: Test any material that is missing a number. Use exactly the same method as before.
flow.say: Some cells are empty. Let's fill them in with the same test, done the same way.
flow.kid: Fill the empty boxes by doing the same tests again.
flow.parent: If a test cannot be done, such as ice melting on a material you do not have, leave the box empty and give that card a 'no data' mark. Honest gaps are better than made-up numbers.

flow.do: 1. For each test, find the biggest number. 2. Give it a score of 5. 3. For every other material, work out its score: multiply its number by 5, then divide by the biggest number. 4. Round to the nearest whole number.
flow.say: The best one in each test gets a 5. For the others, multiply by five and divide by the biggest number. So 5 marbles when the biggest is 22 gives 5 times 5 divided by 22, which is about 1.
flow.kid: The biggest number gets 5. For the others, multiply by 5. Then divide by the biggest. Round it.

check.q: In the strength test the best strip held 22 marbles. Another held 11. About what score should the second get out of 5?
options: 2 or 3, because 11 is about half of 22
check.why: 11 is half of 22, and half of 5 is 2 and a half, so the score is 2 or 3. Picking 5 gives everything a top score. Picking 11 forgets that scores only go up to 5. Making scores like this means every test counts the same.

flow.do: Make the cards. Write the material, draw a picture and write its five scores.
flow.say: Now make your cards. Each one has the material's name, a picture and five scores.
flow.kid: Make your cards. Write the name. Draw a picture. Write the scores.

flow.do: Play your deck like Property Trumps. Compare your card scores with the rough deck.
flow.say: Let's play with our own cards. Then compare them with the rough scores in the first deck.
flow.kid: Play your own cards. Then compare them with the first deck.

flow.do: Ask your child where their scores and the rough deck scores differ, and why.
flow.say: Where do your scores and the rough scores disagree? Which do you trust more, and why?
flow.kid: Where do your scores differ from the first deck? Which do you trust more?
flow.think: Your scores come from tests you did. Why can a test sometimes be more trusted than a guess?

challenges.title: The Mystery Material
challenges.problem: A grown-up has hidden three mystery samples in three numbered bags. You cannot look inside. For each one you have six tests. You must work out what it is like, and make your best guess about what it is.
constraints: You get only six tests for each sample.
You must write down every test before you do it.
You may not tear, cut or break the samples.
materials: three samples in paper bags, such as aluminium foil, waxed paper and a piece of thin plastic
a cup of water, a torch, a fridge magnet, a spoon, a small fork
general: Feel it, bend it, tap it, and see if it floats in water.
Hold it up to the torch to see whether it is transparent, translucent or opaque.
Drip a drop of water on it, to see whether it is waterproof.
Hold it against a fridge magnet. Scratch it gently with a fingernail.
creative: Warm a corner of it between your fingers for ten seconds. Does it soften, or does it stay the same?
Crumple it near your ear, and listen. Papers, foils and plastics each make their own crackle.
Rub it between your fingers. Does it feel cold, waxy or papery?
challenges.your_turn: Now be the one who hides the samples. Choose three, put them in bags, and write clue cards that name properties but not the material. Can your family guess?

flow.do: 1. Give your child the three bags. 2. Explain the rules: six tests for each sample, written down before testing.
flow.say: Each bag holds a mystery material. You can do six tests on each. Choose the tests carefully. Write each one down first.
flow.kid: Three bags hold three mystery materials. You may do six tests on each. Write each test down first.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Mystery Material. It is a detective challenge. You use property tests to work out what hidden materials are like.

flow.do: Help your child write a list of six tests that tell the most. Then do the same for the other two bags.
flow.say: Which six tests will tell you the most? Pick tests that split materials into different groups.
flow.kid: Choose six tests. Make them ones that tell you the most.

good: We only have six.
Some tests tell more than others.
A test that most materials pass tells us little.

flow.do: Do the tests. Write down the result of each in a table. After the last test, write your best guess for each bag.
flow.say: Do the tests. Write down every result. Then write your guess for what each sample is.
flow.kid: Do your tests. Write every result. Then write your best guess.
flow.parent: Good answers: bag 1 shiny, bendy, opaque, waterproof, not magnetic, sinks when crumpled might be foil. Bag 2 translucent, waxy feel and bendy might be waxed paper. Bag 3 clear or cloudy, bendy and stretchy might be thin plastic.

flow.do: Reveal what is in the bags. Ask which test gave the most useful clue.
flow.say: Open the bags. Were you right? Which test told you the most?
flow.kid: Open the bags. Were you right? Which test was the most helpful?
flow.think: Could two different materials give the same results on all six tests? What would you do then?

setup.caption: 2. Write your six tests down before you start.

challenges.title: The Privacy Window
challenges.problem: Your window faces a busy lane. You want sunlight to come in, but you do not want people in the lane to see inside. Use things you find at home to make a model window cover that does both.
constraints: Most of the light must still come through.
A person standing on the other side must not be seen clearly.
You can only use materials from home.
You must test your cover, not guess.
materials: a cardboard frame with a square hole about 20 centimetres wide, as a model window
butter paper, tissue paper, thin cotton, a plastic sheet, newspaper, a sheet of foil
scissors, sticky tape, a torch, a pencil
a friend to stand on the other side
general: Stick butter paper or tracing paper over the hole. It is translucent, so it lets in light but blurs the picture.
Layer thin tissue paper, a sheet at a time, until the person is just a shape.
Hang a net or a thin cotton curtain over the window.
creative: Cut a pattern of small holes, like an Indian jaali screen. Light and air come through, but eyes cannot see a clear picture.
Make a bamboo blind, with thin slats close together. People call these chick blinds in many Indian homes.
Hang a khus tatti, a mat of woven grass. In summer, people sprinkle it with water, and it cools the air that comes through.
Stick thin coloured tissue paper in a pattern, like stained glass, and see what the light does.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own cover. Draw it, make it and test it. How much light did it let in? How well did it hide the person?

flow.do: 1. Make the cardboard frame with a square hole. 2. Ask your friend to stand on the other side and hold up a picture or a face. 3. Look through the empty frame. Everything is clear.
flow.say: This is our window. Look through the empty frame. You can see everything. How can we hide the person but keep the light?
flow.kid: This is your model window. Look through it. You can see everything. How can you hide the person and keep the light?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Privacy Window. It is a design challenge. You find a material that lets light in but hides what is behind it.

flow.do: 1. Try covering the hole with one material at a time. 2. Shine the torch from behind, and look from the front. 3. Write down: how much light? How clear is the person?
flow.say: Try each material over the hole. Ask two things each time. How much light comes in? How clearly can I see the person?
flow.kid: Cover the hole with each material. Ask: how much light? How clear is the person?
flow.parent: Good results: butter paper and thin cotton make a translucent window. Foil is opaque. A clear plastic sheet is transparent and hides nothing.

flow.do: Combine ideas. Try layers of tissue. Try a jaali pattern. Try two materials together.
flow.say: Can you combine two ideas? One layer of butter paper with a pattern of small holes? Test it.
flow.kid: Try layers. Try a jaali pattern. Try two ideas together. Test each.

ask.q: What happened when you added more layers?
good: It let in less light.
The person was harder to see.
There is a balance: enough layers to hide, not so many that it goes dark.

flow.do: Choose the best cover. Say why it works, using the words transparent, translucent and opaque.
flow.say: Which cover is best? Tell me why, using our three light words.
flow.kid: Which cover works best? Say why, using transparent, translucent and opaque.
flow.think: Old houses in India used jaali screens and khus tatti. What problems did they solve at the same time?

quiz.p: Which of these is a property of a material?
quiz.why: A property tells what a material is like, and waterproof does that. A spoon is an object. A kitchen and a shop are places. Picking 'a spoon' mixes up the thing with the stuff it is made of.

quiz.p: A steel spoon and a steel tumbler are different objects. What is the same about them?
quiz.why: Both are steel, so both are hard, shiny and cold to touch. Picking shape, use or size mixes up the object and the material. Those are properties of the object, not of the steel.

quiz.p: A fingernail scratches chalk. A steel nail scratches a fingernail. Which is hardest?
quiz.why: If A scratches B, then A is harder than B. The nail scratches the fingernail, and the fingernail scratches the chalk. So the nail is hardest and the chalk is softest. Picking the chalk reverses the clue.
quiz.context: This is the scratch test. If one thing can scratch another, the first is harder.

quiz.p: Strip A drooped 2 centimetres in the droop test. Strip B drooped 9 centimetres. Which is more flexible?
quiz.why: A big drop means the strip bent a lot, so B is more flexible. A drooped only a little, so it is more rigid. Picking A is the common mistake of thinking a smaller number is more bendy.

quiz.p: In the strength test, newspaper held 5 marbles and cloth held 15. How many times as many marbles did the cloth hold?
quiz.why: 15 divided by 5 is 3. So the cloth held 3 times as many marbles. Picking 10 is what you get by subtracting, 15 take away 5. But 'how many times' needs division.

quiz.p: Glass is the right material for a window and the wrong one for a bridge. Why?
opts: The job decides which properties matter
Bridges are not made of anything
quiz.why: A window needs see-through. A bridge needs strong. Glass is see-through but brittle. No property is good or bad by itself. Picking 'glass is a bad material' misses that glass is perfect for its own job.

quiz.p: In the story, cotton thread held 11 seeds in the damp dawn and 6 at noon. What did Shefali find out?
opts: Cotton thread is stronger when it is damp
The seeds were heavier at noon
quiz.why: She kept the thread, the length and the seeds the same. Only the dampness changed. A damp noon thread held 9. So damp makes cotton stronger. Picking 'angry river' or 'tired thread' are guesses with no test behind them.
quiz.context: In The Thread That Held at Dawn, a girl counted red seeds hung from threads at dawn and at noon.

quiz.p: A glass bangle is hard to scratch but breaks when dropped. It is…
quiz.why: Hard is about scratching. Brittle is about snapping. Glass is both hard and brittle. Picking 'strong' mixes up hard and strong.

quiz.p: Which word means springs back after being stretched?
quiz.why: Elastic things, like rubber bands, spring back. Brittle things snap. Opaque means no light passes. Rigid means stiff and not bendy.

quiz.p: Ice melted fastest on the steel plate and slowest on folded wool. What does this show about steel?
quiz.why: Steel is a conductor of heat. It let room heat flow into the ice quickly. Wool traps air and carries heat slowly. Picking 'colder' is the common idea, but if it were colder the ice would last longer.

quiz.p: Diamond and pencil lead are both made of carbon. Why is diamond so much harder?
opts: The atoms are joined in a different pattern
quiz.why: The pattern of joins decides the property. In diamond every atom is locked to four neighbours. In graphite the atoms are in flat sheets that slide. Picking 'bigger atoms' is a natural guess, but the atoms are the same.

quiz.p: One sheet of butter paper is translucent. A tall stack of butter paper is opaque. What does this show?
opts: A property can change with thickness
Translucent and opaque mean the same
quiz.why: Each layer scatters and soaks up some light. With more layers, less comes through. So thickness changes the property. Picking 'two materials' is not true, because it is the same paper.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still not fully understand?
opts: What exactly glass is, and why a liquid turns into glass
That a steel nail is harder than chalk
That wet cotton is stronger than dry
quiz.why: Glass is an open puzzle. Its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's but stuck like a solid's. A famous physicist called it one of the deepest unsolved problems of solid matter. The other three have been tested again and again.

quiz.p: Tissue paper tears very easily. Is that always a bad property?
opts: No, it depends on the job
Yes, because paper should be strong
No, because tissue paper is not a material
quiz.why: Tissue paper tears easily, and that is useful for wrapping a gift that must be opened. Weak is only bad when the job needs strong. Picking 'always bad' treats a property as good or bad on its own.

quiz.p: A steel spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon in the same room. What is the best explanation?
opts: Steel takes heat from your hand faster
quiz.why: Both are at room temperature. Your skin feels how fast heat leaves your hand, and steel pulls it away faster. Picking 'steel is a lower temperature' is the common idea. A thermometer would show the same number for both.

applications: Kitchens use steel for pans and wooden or plastic for handles, because steel carries heat and wood and plastic do not.
Raincoats and umbrellas are plastic or coated cloth, because they must be waterproof.
Towels and dishcloths are cotton, because cotton is absorbent.
Windows are glass, because glass is transparent. Bathroom windows are frosted, because translucent glass lets in light but hides us.
Bridges and railway lines use steel, because steel is both strong and hard.
Cricket bats are made of willow wood, which is strong but a little springy and does not split.
Wires are copper or aluminium, because metals carry electricity and heat well. Their covering is plastic, which does not.
Jewellers use a heat probe to tell a diamond from glass, because a diamond carries heat much faster.
Builders in dry places use clay or stone for thick walls. These are poor conductors of heat, so rooms stay cool.
Engineers choose bamboo for scaffolding in India because it is strong and flexible and cheap.
Mattresses and pillows use foam or cotton, because soft, springy materials are comfortable.
Safety helmets and shoes use hard shells and soft padding, because each material does a different job.
Geologists test rocks with a scratch test and a hand lens. They use the Mohs scale in the field.
Space agencies, including ISRO, choose materials for rockets and landers that stay strong in heat, cold and vibration.
Doctors use materials in the body, like steel and plastic joints and dental fillings. These must be strong, safe and not rust.

open_questions.q: What exactly is glass? Is it a solid, a very slow liquid, or something else?
open_questions.why_open: Glass has atoms jumbled like a liquid's but stuck in place like a solid's. A famous physicist, Philip Anderson, wrote in 1995 that the nature of glass may be the deepest unsolved problem in solid physics. Scientists still argue about why a liquid turns into glass when it cools. And old windows are not flowing.

open_questions.q: Can we work out a material's properties before we make it?
open_questions.why_open: In 2023, a computer program from Google DeepMind predicted 2.2 million new crystals, and 380,000 looked stable. Some chemists said many were not really new or useful. Nobody knows yet how many will turn out to be good materials.

open_questions.q: Is there a material harder than diamond?
open_questions.why_open: Computer models say a rare form of diamond with a different atom pattern, called lonsdaleite, could be harder. It is named after Kathleen Lonsdale. In 2014 other scientists said that natural samples are not a separate material. Whether a pure one can be made is still argued.

open_questions.q: How does a spider spin silk so tough, from water and a fly's meal, at room temperature?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have copied the chemical recipe, but nobody has yet made fibre as good as the real thing, in large amounts, without a spider.

open_questions.q: What is the strongest material that can possibly exist?
open_questions.why_open: Graphene is the strongest ever measured. A computer model says nuclear pasta, inside a neutron star, could be far stronger. Nobody knows whether anything stronger could exist, or could ever be made.

open_questions.q: Can we make materials that mend themselves, like skin?
open_questions.why_open: Some plastics and concretes in laboratories can close small cracks. None yet matches living things, which heal again and again for decades.

open_questions.q: Why is hardness so hard to define?
open_questions.why_open: Scratching, denting and bouncing back are different tests, and they do not always give the same order. Scientists use several hardness scales. There is still no single number that means 'hard'.

open_questions.q: What properties are there that we have not yet thought to test?
open_questions.why_open: Strength, hardness and shine were noticed long ago. Others, like how a material behaves at one atom thick, were only found when new tools arrived. We cannot know what we have not yet looked for.

maths.problem: In the droop test, a thick card strip dropped 3 centimetres. A paper strip dropped 12 centimetres. How many times as far did the paper drop?
maths.explain: The card dropped 3 centimetres and the paper dropped 12. 12 divided by 3 is 4. So the paper dropped 4 times as far. You can check: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12.
maths.context: The droop test measures how bendy a strip is. You let 10 centimetres of a strip stick out over a table edge, and measure how far its tip drops. A bigger drop means a bendier strip.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how far each strip dropped
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show how the problem works.

maths.why_maths: Scientists do not just say 'the paper is bendier'. They ask 'how many times bendier?' Dividing one number by the other gives the answer.

maths.problem: In the scratch test, the candle wax scratched 0 things, the soap 1, the chalk 2, the fingernail 3 and the steel nail 4. Draw a bar chart. Then say which is the second hardest.
maths.answer: The fingernail is the second hardest. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each, as tall as its score. Put the scores in order, from tallest to shortest: 4, 3, 2, 1, 0. The tallest bar is the steel nail. The next tallest is the fingernail, with 3. So the fingernail is second hardest.
maths.context: In the scratch test, you try to scratch each thing with each of the others. Each thing's score is how many others it scratched. A higher score means a harder thing.

answer_chart.title: Scores from the scratch test
answer_chart.y: Number of other things it scratched
answer_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show how the problem works.

maths.why_maths: A bar chart turns a list of scores into a picture. The tallest bar shows the winner at a glance, and the order shows the ladder.

maths.problem: In the strength test, a cloth strip held 14 marbles. Suppose each marble weighs 5 grams. How many grams did the cloth hold?
maths.explain: Each marble weighs 5 grams, and there were 14 of them. 14 times 5 is 70. You can check: 10 marbles are 50 grams, and 4 more marbles are 20 grams. 50 + 20 = 70.
maths.context: The strength test hangs a cup from a strip of material and adds marbles until the strip tears. The number of marbles shows how strong the strip is.
maths.why_maths: Counting marbles is a start. Changing the count into grams, a unit everyone shares, lets other people compare their results with ours.

maths.problem: In the ice race, the ice melted in 14 minutes on the steel plate and in 38 minutes on the folded wool. How many more minutes did it take on the wool?
maths.explain: The wool took 38 minutes and the steel took 14. 38 take away 14 is 24. You can check: 14 + 24 = 38.
maths.context: The ice race puts identical ice cubes on different materials and times how long each takes to melt. A longer time means the material carries heat more slowly.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how many minutes each ice cube took to melt
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show how the problem works.

maths.why_maths: Taking one time from another tells us how much longer the wool kept the ice. That difference is the evidence for the claim that wool is a better insulator.

maths.problem: Aarav sorted 12 things into two rings. 7 things were hard. 5 things were shiny. 3 things were both hard and shiny. How many things were neither?
maths.explain: The 3 things that are both are counted once in the hard group and once in the shiny group. So the number of things that are hard or shiny is 7 + 5 take away 3, which is 9. 12 take away 9 leaves 3 things that are neither.
maths.context: In the two-ring sort, you put things into a ring for HARD and a ring for SHINY. The rings overlap in the middle for things that are both.
maths.why_maths: When groups overlap, we must be careful not to count the middle twice. Two overlapping rings are the picture that makes this clear.

maths.problem: Look at the ruler in the picture. It shows how far a paper strip dropped in the droop test. Each small mark is one centimetre. What is the reading?
maths.explain: The tip of the strip reaches the mark after 6 and before 8. It sits on the mark between them, which is 7. So the strip dropped 7 centimetres.
maths.context: In the droop test, you hold a ruler upright beside the table edge and read how far the tip of a strip has dropped.

chart.label: Each small mark is one centimetre.

maths.why_maths: A measuring tool only helps if you can read it. Reading the mark where the tip touches turns the picture into a number you can compare.

roots.context: We have been learning about properties, the words for what a material is like. Now we ask what properties tell us about ourselves and the world.

three.who_am_i: Your bones are hard and your skin is bendy. You have many properties too.
three.what_is_life: Bone, wood and shell are materials that living things grow and mend.
three.what_is_this_world: A diamond and pencil lead are both pure carbon. Same atoms, different ways.

roots.thread: A diamond is one of the hardest things there is. Pencil lead is one of the softest. Both are made of exactly the same carbon atoms, only joined in different ways. DeepKids believes this is the One showing up as the many. The same stuff, arranged differently, becomes hard or soft, clear or shiny. Properties are how one world shows its many faces.

teachings.teaching: Nagarjuna taught that nothing exists all by itself. Everything is what it is because of other things.
teachings.link: Glass is hard compared to chalk, and soft compared to diamond. Hardness is not inside the glass alone. It shows up when one thing meets another.

teachings.source: The Jain teaching of anekantavada, many-sidedness
teachings.teaching: Jain thinkers taught that every thing has many sides. Each view sees some of the truth, but never all of it.
teachings.link: A thread can be weak for one job and right for another. One material has many properties, and the job decides which one matters.

science.text: A material's properties come from its atoms and how they are joined. Diamond and graphite, the black part of a pencil, are both pure carbon.
Glass is a solid whose atoms are jumbled, like a frozen liquid. Exactly how a liquid turns into glass is still argued about.

other_view.view: Many scientists say a property is fully explained by atoms and the way they join. Nothing more is needed. On this view, the One is a beautiful idea, but not part of the explanation.

practice.title: Listen to the materials
